content: Estradiol and norethindrone acetate, delivered via a transdermal patch, is a combination of estrogen and progestin approved by the FDA for the treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause, moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal atrophy due to menopause, and hypoestrogenism caused by hypogonadism, castration, or primary ovarian failure. Common side effects include edema, irritation at the application site, chloasma, hirsutism, scalp hair loss, persistent skin erythema, pruritus, weight gain, abdominal pain, bloating, headache, breast tenderness, menstrual disorders, breast pain or swelling, vaginal discomfort, withdrawal bleeding, upper respiratory infections, and general pain. Adult Indications and Dosage Initiation of Therapy: Therapy should begin at the lowest effective dose. Estrogens, with or without progestins, should be prescribed at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals and individual risk factors. The lowest effective dose of estradiol/norethindrone acetate has not been established in clinical trials. Women not currently on continuous estrogen or combination estrogen-progestin therapy may start estradiol/norethindrone acetate at any time. Women already on continuous therapy should complete their current cycle before transitioning to estradiol/norethindrone acetate. Withdrawal bleeding often occurs at the end of the cycle, and the first day of bleeding is an appropriate time to begin therapy. Therapeutic Regimens: Combination estrogen-progestin regimens are indicated for women with an intact uterus. The lowest effective dose should be used. Women should be re-evaluated every 3 to 6 months to determine if continued hormone therapy is appropriate. The patch is applied to the lower abdomen and replaced twice weekly during a 28-day cycle. Irregular bleeding may occur initially but typically decreases over time, often leading to amenorrhea. Contraindications Estradiol/norethindrone acetate is contraindicated in women with: Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding. Known, suspected, or history of breast cancer. Known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia. Active or history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE). Active or history of arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction). Known hypersensitivity to estradiol/norethindrone acetate. Known liver impairment or disease. Known protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders. Known or suspected pregnancy. Warnings Thromboembolic Events: Estrogen plus progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of PE, DVT, stroke, and myocardial infarction (MI). Estrogen-alone therapy has been linked to an increased risk of stroke and DVT. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if any of these conditions occur or are suspected. Endometrial Cancer: Unopposed estrogen therapy in women with a uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer. Adding a progestin reduces this risk. Breast Cancer: Estrogen plus progestin therapy has been associated with an increased risk of invasive breast cancer. Women should undergo regular breast examinations and mammography based on age and risk factors. Ovarian Cancer: Some studies suggest an increased risk of ovarian cancer with prolonged use of estrogen or estrogen-progestin therapy. Dementia: Women aged 65 and older on estrogen or estrogen-progestin therapy may have an increased risk of probable dementia. Gallbladder Disease: Estrogen therapy has been associated with an increased risk of gallbladder disease requiring surgery. Hypercalcemia: Estrogen therapy may exacerbate hypercalcemia in patients with breast cancer and bone metastases. Visual Abnormalities: Retinal vascular thrombosis has been reported. Therapy should be discontinued if sudden vision loss or other visual symptoms occur. Hereditary Angioedema: Exogenous estrogens may worsen symptoms of hereditary angioedema. Precautions Progestin Addition: Adding a progestin to estrogen therapy reduces the risk of endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor to endometrial cancer. However, progestin use may increase the risk of breast cancer. Blood Pressure: Estrogen therapy has not been shown to have a generalized effect on blood pressure, but idiosyncratic reactions causing significant increases have been reported. Hypertriglyceridemia: Estrogen therapy may elevate plasma triglycerides, leading to pancreatitis in women with preexisting hypertriglyceridemia. Hepatic Impairment: Estrogens may be poorly metabolized in women with liver dysfunction. Therapy should be discontinued if cholestatic jaundice recurs. Hypothyroidism: Estrogen therapy increases thyroid-binding globulin levels, potentially requiring higher doses of thyroid hormone replacement in hypothyroid women. Fluid Retention: Estrogens and progestins may cause fluid retention, necessitating caution in women with conditions such as cardiac or renal impairment. Hypocalcemia: Estrogen therapy should be used cautiously in women with hypoparathyroidism, as it may induce hypocalcemia. Exacerbation of Conditions: Estrogen therapy may worsen asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, migraines, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas. Adverse Reactions Genitourinary System: Endometrial hyperplasia, uterine leiomyomata, and uterine spasms. Breast: Breast cancer. Cardiovascular: Hypertension and varicose veins. Gastrointestinal: Cholestatic jaundice, gallbladder disorders, and elevated transaminases. Skin: Skin discoloration. Central Nervous System: Mood changes, libido disorders, migraines, vertigo, and paresthesia. Miscellaneous: Angioedema, hypersensitivity, and weight gain. Drug Interactions Estrogens are metabolized by cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4). Inducers of CYP3A4 (e.g., St. John’s Wort, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, rifampin) may reduce estrogen levels, decreasing therapeutic effects. Inhibitors of CYP3A4 (e.g., erythromycin, ketoconazole, grapefruit juice) may increase estrogen levels, potentially causing side effects. Administration and Monitoring The transdermal patch should be applied to a clean, dry, and smooth area of the lower abdomen, avoiding the breasts and waistline. Application sites should be rotated, with at least one week between applications to the same site. The patch should not be exposed to prolonged sunlight. If the patch becomes dislodged, it can be reapplied or replaced, maintaining the original treatment schedule. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Estradiol/norethindrone acetate should not be used during pregnancy. Nursing Mothers: Estrogen therapy may reduce the quantity and quality of breast milk and should be avoided during lactation. Pediatric Use: Not indicated for children. Geriatric Use: Limited data are available for women over 65 years of age. Studies suggest an increased risk of stroke, breast cancer, and dementia in this population.
